area.title: Witness Square
area.subtitle: What can we know about events we did not see?
area.blurb: Historians cannot rerun the past. They weigh sources, time, and motive.
area.intro: The old courthouse still faces the square. On the bench, the question is not “Can I feel this?” but “What kind of testimony is this, and what would a fair historian do with it?”
Christian faith is not only inward. It makes a public claim: Jesus of Nazareth died, was buried, and was reported alive by people who said they had seen him.
These challenges teach method as much as conclusion. Early, multiple, and costly testimony is not a laboratory proof — it is the kind of evidence history actually has.

lesson.title: What Paul received
lesson.idea: died, buried, raised, appeared — in that order
lesson.claim: Paul hands on an early public creed: died, buried, raised, appeared.
lesson.plain: Paul hands on an old shared belief: died, buried, raised, appeared.

journal.title: Of first importance
journal.body: 1 Corinthians 15:3–5 is a compressed public claim: death, burial, raising, appearances. Paul presents it as received tradition, not as a private dream. Burial resists a merely “spiritual” death; appearances resist a merely “spiritual” raising.
This is what the churches were already handing on when Paul wrote — a mid-first-century letter appealing to a still-earlier formula.

easy.learn: This is not Paul’s private dream. He says the churches were already saying it: Christ died, was buried, was raised, and was seen.

match.sentence: Paul hands on an early public creed: died, buried, raised, appeared.

hold.why: Buried and seen — not only a spirit story.
hold.claimMiss: The creed is Paul’s private dream from decades later.
Paul invented the formula on the spot in Corinth.
hold.whyMiss: “Buried” is only poetic decoration.
Appearances are admitted to be visions with no named people.

lesson.title: Why historians call it early
lesson.idea: the creed is early testimony, not a medieval insert
lesson.claim: The resurrection claim sits close to the events, not as a late legend.
lesson.plain: That old shared belief is early testimony, not a medieval insert.

journal.title: Early is not the same as easy
journal.body: Historians cannot rewind the world. They ask how close a report stands to the events, how formulaic it is, and whether the author is appealing to known people (Cephas, the Twelve, James, a large group, Paul himself).
Luke 1:1–4 shows another first-century Christian writer claiming the posture of inquiry among eyewitnesses. That posture can be tested. It stands to be weighed.

easy.learn: Paul wrote in the mid-first century. He says he received this core and passed it on. That is close to the events — not a monk’s later add-on.

match.sentence: The resurrection claim sits close to the events, not as a late legend.

hold.why: Paul names known people who saw it.
hold.claimMiss: Early is the same as laboratory proof.
No first-century writer claims to have asked witnesses.
hold.whyMiss: Named people make a report less testable.
Distance in time is the only historical question that matters.

medium.learn: Paul quotes a received formula and names known people; Luke claims inquiry among witnesses.

lesson.title: Tools of the ancient historian
lesson.idea: historians weigh sources; they cannot rerun the past
lesson.claim: Ordinary historical tools weigh testimony; they do not replace reading.
lesson.plain: Historians weigh sources. They cannot rerun the past.

journal.title: How the past is weighed
journal.body: Multiple attestation, embarrassment, early testimony, and contextual credibility are ordinary tools. They do not replace reading. They resist the story that every Christian report is a late pious novel.
Used honestly, they also resist the opposite laziness: “an early creed is already a laboratory proof.” History gives testimony, not a rerun.
journal.cite: Standard historical method as used in ancient history and historical Jesus studies

easy.learn: Ask: how many reports? How awkward is the detail? How soon was it said? Does it fit that world? Those tools test a report. They are not a chemistry lab.

match.sentence: Ordinary historical tools weigh testimony; they do not replace reading.

hold.why: Many early, awkward reports beat a late tale.
hold.claimMiss: An early creed is already a laboratory proof.
Every Christian report is automatically a late novel.
hold.whyMiss: Method is a way to skip the texts themselves.
Embarrassment means a story must be false.

lesson.title: Idle talk
lesson.idea: women as first witnesses is an awkward detail to invent
lesson.claim: The first tomb reports begin with women — an awkward opening if invented for respectability.
lesson.plain: Women as first witnesses is an awkward detail to invent.

journal.title: Awkward beginnings
journal.body: The tomb stories begin with women, and Luke records that the apostles dismissed them (Luke 24:11). That is an odd opening if the only goal is later public respectability.

Outside the Gospels, Tacitus (Annals 15.44) notes Christus executed under Pilate and a movement that spread to Rome. Josephus (Antiquities 18.63–64) is partly disputed because of later Christian touches, and honesty about that dispute belongs in the dossier.

easy.learn: The tomb stories begin with women. Luke says the men called it idle talk. If you only wanted later respect, you would more likely lead with respected men.

match.sentence: The first tomb reports begin with women — an awkward opening if invented for respectability.

hold.why: The men first called the women wrong.
hold.claimMiss: The Gospels open with the Roman senate converting overnight.
Women were the most legally impressive public witnesses.
hold.whyMiss: Luke sands away any dismissal of the first report.
Outside writers never mention Christus or Pilate.

medium.learn: Luke records that the apostles dismissed them — a costly opening if the goal were instant respectability.
